title: Nothing Runs While You're Gone
dek: A build timer in Clash of Clans is one integer on one row. It is also the cheapest server design anyone has found for a game with a hundred million players, and the mechanism that decides when you next open the app. This is a short note on how the two halves are the same object: the state model that makes these games nearly free to run is the state model that makes them hard to put down — and where that stops being a fair trade.
byline: 28 September 2026 · Inferred from shipped behaviour and public talks, not from anyone's source tree
description: How simple mobile games model their state — lazy timers, per-player documents, command sourcing, replays — and how the same structures produce the retention loop.
og_description: Clash of Clans and its relatives store a village as a few kilobytes, run nothing in the background, resolve every timer lazily on login, and replay battles from a snapshot plus a command list. This note works through those structures, shows why they are orders of magnitude cheaper than a tick loop, and then argues that the same timestamp that makes the backend cheap is the appointment that brings the player back — with an honest section on where that becomes extractive.
twitter_description: The cheapest way to store a mobile game is a timestamp. So is the strongest way to schedule a player's return. A short note on why those are the same design.

How to read the badges

I have not seen any of these games' source. from the record marks something publicly documented or directly observable in a shipped client — a published talk, a stated design, behaviour anyone can reproduce by playing. reconstruction marks mechanism I have inferred from that behaviour, which is a guess with reasons and may be wrong in its details. computed here marks arithmetic done for this page from the assumptions printed beside it. Where a number would have to come from a company's internal dashboard, I have left it out rather than invent it.

sections.title: One object, two jobs
figures: fig-thesis · the same field read twice (SVG) · one finish_at column, read by the server as work-to-skip and by the player as an appointment
sections.brief: Thesis up front: finish_at is simultaneously the cheapest possible server representation of an in-progress upgrade and the scheduling primitive for the player's next session. Set up the two halves of the note and say plainly that the second half is where the ethics live.

sections.title: The village is a small document
figures: fig-village · the player record (SVG, wide) · field-by-field layout with byte counts, and the config table it points into
sections.brief: Per-player state is one owner-scoped document: buildings as (type id, x, y, level, finish_at), resources with last_collected, army, progression counters. Balance data lives in shipped config tables keyed by (type, level), not in the save. Consequences: a balance change is a data deploy not a migration; saves stay tiny; the whole population fits in memory on a modest fleet. Computed sizes.

sections.title: Nothing runs while you are gone
figures: fig-lazy · two designs, same game (SVG, wide) · a tick loop over every player against lazy resolution on login, with the computed ops-per-second for each
sections.brief: The load-bearing trick: an upgrade is not a job on a queue, it is a timestamp; a resource pile is not incremented on a schedule, it is a closed-form integral of rate times elapsed, clamped at capacity. Work happens only when someone looks. Computed comparison. Note the two things this buys beyond cost: no drift, and trivially correct behaviour across downtime.

sections.title: One player, one actor
figures: fig-actor · ownership map (SVG) · player actors, the clan actor, and the one place shared mutable state exists
sections.brief: Single-threaded ownership per player: state in memory, mutations serialised, periodic persistence. No locks in the core loop because there is nothing to contend over. The clan is the only genuinely shared object and it is deliberately weakly consistent — chat, donations, war are eventual and idempotent. Reconstruction badge on the internals; the observable behaviour is the evidence.

sections.title: Commands, not state
figures: fig-replay · a battle as data (SVG, wide) · defender snapshot plus timestamped command list plus deterministic engine, with sizes against a video recording
sections.brief: Clients send commands with a tick number, not state. A deterministic simulation shared by client and server means the server can re-run the battle to validate it, and a replay is a snapshot plus a command list — kilobytes, not megabytes. Async PvP: you attack a snapshot, not a person, which is why nobody has to be online. Matchmaking becomes a lookup in a sorted index. Note what determinism costs: floating point discipline, versioned config, no wall-clock reads in the sim.

sections.title: Loops inside loops
figures: fig-loops · periods, drawn to scale (SVG, wide) · five nested loops from thirty seconds to a season, each with its own reward and its own reason to come back
sections.brief: The attention architecture stated structurally: a game is several loops with different periods running at once, and the design rule is that at least one loop should be closing whenever the player opens the app. Name the periods with examples. The point to make: this is scheduling, not persuasion — the psychology is in the next section, the structure is here.

sections.title: The timer economy
figures: fig-ladder · a day of appointments (SVG, wide) · a timer ladder turning into a notification schedule and a session count
fig-gems · time priced as money (SVG) · the convex skip curve and the two-currency loop, explicitly illustrative
sections.brief: Timers are appointments. Caps create urgency without loss. The two-currency structure exists so that hard currency buys back time, which makes the length of a timer a pricing decision. Derive the constraint: too short and there is nothing to sell, too long and the player leaves. Loss aversion and shields. Variable rewards. Then the retention arithmetic: expected lifetime is one over daily churn, so small changes to the daily loop move lifetime a lot — computed, and the reason studios obsess over it.

sections.title: Where it turns extractive
figures: fig-line · promise or trap (table) · mechanic by mechanic, what it offers, and the version of it that crosses the line
sections.brief: The honest section. A test: does the mechanic make a promise the player can plan around, or does it manufacture a cost for not showing up? Timers and seasons are promises; streaks that reset, limited-time offers with fake countdowns, pay-to-avoid-loss, randomised paid rewards aimed at minors are not. Note the regulatory record on loot boxes without overclaiming the details, and the whale-revenue concentration pattern that shapes the incentive. State my own position briefly and move on.

sections.title: What the rest of us should steal
figures: fig-steal · four transplants (SVG, wide) · lazy accrual, command sourcing, owner-scoped documents and honest appointments, each with where it fits outside games
sections.brief: The engineering transplants are excellent and mostly free: lazy accrual instead of cron for anything that is a function of elapsed time; commands with sequence numbers instead of state PUTs; owner-scoped documents so the hot path never needs a transaction; a deterministic core so you can replay for audit. Then the product transplant, stated carefully: appointments are legitimate when the thing genuinely finishes and the user set it. Tie to agent work — a long-running job is a finish_at, and a notification you asked for is not a dark pattern.
